title: Lang–Plaut problem
formal: For every integer \(K\geq2\), do there exist a finite integer \(N(K)\geq1\) and a finite real constant \(D(K)\geq1\) such that every \(K\)-doubling subset \(X\) of real Hilbert space admits a map \(F:X\to\mathbb R^{N(K)}\) satisfying \[\|x-y\|_2\leq\|F(x)-F(y)\|_2\leq D(K)\|x-y\|_2\qquad(x,y\in X)?\]
why: The problem asks whether intrinsic local metric dimension completely controls Euclidean dimensional reduction once Hilbert embeddability is available. Its resolution would clarify a central obstruction to finite-dimensional metric representation and the limits of geometry-based compression independent of dataset size.
status_note: Open in the checked Naor–Neiman and Lafforgue–Naor sources. A bounded later-work search on 13 September 2026 did not identify a resolution for the Hilbert case. Results for other Banach spaces or restricted families do not supply one; this is not an exhaustive current-openness certification.

importance.reason: A major metric-embedding characterization problem: whether doubling and Hilbert embeddability suffice for finite-dimensional Euclidean representation.

category_assignment.reason: Category from the approved fundamental-problem proposal

sentences: A doubling metric has uniformly limited local branching: each ball can be covered by a bounded number of smaller balls.
The Lang–Plaut problem considers such a metric when it already sits inside a Hilbert space.
It asks whether the points can be represented in some finite-dimensional Euclidean space while changing all distances by only a bounded factor.
Both dimension and distortion should depend only on the doubling constant.
The issue is whether intrinsic metric simplicity suffices to eliminate an infinite-dimensional ambient representation.

definitions: It suffices to use the real Hilbert space \(\ell_2=\{(x_i)_{i\geq1}:\sum_i x_i^2<\infty\}\), with norm \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_i x_i^2)^{1/2}\). A doubling subset of any Hilbert space is separable and isometrically identifies with a subset of this space. Give \(X\subseteq\ell_2\) the restricted Hilbert distance. It is \(K\)-doubling if, for every \(x\in X\) and \(r>0\), the closed ball \(B_X(x,r)=\{y\in X:\|x-y\|_2\leq r\}\) is covered by at most \(K\) closed balls \(B_X(z,r/2)\) with centers \(z\in X\). No boundedness, closedness, compactness or finiteness of \(X\) is assumed. Empty sets and singletons cause no difficulty. The codomain has its ordinary Euclidean norm. The displayed lower inequality makes the map injective and fixes its arbitrary scale; without that normalization, distortion is the product of the Lipschitz constants of a map and its inverse on its image. The functions \(N,D\) must be chosen before \(X\), and may depend only on \(K\), not on the number of points, diameter, aspect ratio or ambient Hilbert dimension. The embedding may be nonlinear and may be chosen separately for each \(X\). There is no algorithm, continuity beyond the displayed bounds, or prescribed polynomial dependence on \(K\) required. Distances themselves must be preserved within these factors; replacing them by a power smaller than one changes the target.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal statement in Lean, or give a complete Lean-checked refutation with a fixed doubling bound for which no uniform pair of finite dimension and distortion bounds works. Equivalently, the qualitative Lang–Plaut formulation can be settled by proving that every doubling Hilbert subset has some finite-dimensional bi-Lipschitz embedding, or by exhibiting one that has none; the source proves the equivalence with the quantitative formulation. A restriction to linear maps, snowflaked distances, or bounds growing with the number of points does not resolve the question.

context_blocks.text: Naor and Neiman state the Lang–Plaut question in Section 1.1 and justify its quantitative form in Section 4. This card uses that form so the dependence of dimension and distortion is explicit. The original question is attributed there to Lang and Plaut’s Question 2.4.

Every subset of a fixed-dimensional Euclidean space is doubling, with a bound controlled by dimension, and is already a subset of Hilbert space. A positive answer would make these two necessary conditions sufficient for finite-dimensional bi-Lipschitz embeddability.

Naor and Neiman prove that for an arbitrary doubling metric \((X,d)\), every snowflake \((X,d^{1-\eta})\), \(0<\eta<1/2\), embeds into a Euclidean space whose dimension depends only on the doubling constant. The distortion still depends on \(\eta\). Letting \(\eta\) tend to zero therefore does not supply the uniformly controlled embedding asked for here.

Lafforgue and Naor construct, for every \(p>2\), a doubling subset of \(L_p\) that has no bi-Lipschitz embedding into any finite-dimensional Euclidean space. Their theorem explicitly leaves the Hilbert case \(p=2\) open, so replacing Hilbert space by a general Banach space changes the answer.

Usual finite-set dimension reduction allows dimension to grow with the logarithm of the number of points. Here arbitrarily large or infinite sets with the same doubling bound must share a finite target dimension and distortion bound. This is a geometric existence question rather than a request for a faster implementation of a known projection.
